speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The hope for many of us is that both the US and China find a way to co-exist together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the two largest economic powers, their peaceful co-existence could allow Asia and the rest of the world to continue to prosper in peace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, this rivalry seems to have grown and intensified over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Last year, US Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan in the face of objections and threats of dire consequences from China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The message she wanted to send as clear – that the US stands firmly behind its ally, Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China responded with joint military exercises in the Taiwan straits and unprecedented missile overflights over Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While this rivalry had started out as a largely economic one, the risk of a military confrontation has suddenly also become more real.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The economic rivalry itself should not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, there was a wave of US investment into China and trade from China with the world blossomed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was like a golden age for economic prosperity following the end of the Cold War.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The last few years though have marked a sharp reversal of this trend.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the rivalry between China and the US intensified, US companies have started leaving China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Amazon, Yahoo and Linked In are the latest companies to announce exits from China, following Google which exited more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Prior to this, other well-known names such as Macy’s, Home Depot, eBay and Best Buy have entered and exited China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Chinese company Huawei was hit with restrictions in 2019 and China followed with its own restrictions on various US sectors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Following US sanctions on Hong Kong lawmakers in the wake of the unrest there, China had responded with sanctions on US lawmakers too, including members of President Trump’s administration and lawmakers, such as Senators Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This rivalry has also manifested itself in the realm of critical technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, the US last year imposed restrictions on the sales of advanced semiconductor chips, especially those with wide applications in artificial intelligence (AI) to China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What are the key risks and challenges for Singapore and the region arising from intensifying US-China competition?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: US-China relations are vital for regional peace and prosperity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore has always welcome both countries' efforts to keep communication channels open and engaged in dialogues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The recent balloon incidents seem to suggest that the space or window of opportunity is closing again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While we are a small nation, we can still play our part.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What is the prognosis and are there opportunities for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: US-China relations, which set the tone for global affairs, are worsening.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Neither side expect relations to improve anytime soon and there is a risk of things worsening quickly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This assessment was a marked difference in tone compared to the Prime Minister’s speech on US-China relations at the 2019 International Institute for Strategic Studies keynote address and the Prime Minister’s essay on US-China relations in Foreign Affairs magazine in 2020.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the aftermath of the recent shoot-down of a Chinese balloon over the US, there were reports of the visit of a senior Pentagon official to Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Taiwan is likely to be a focus of contention in US-China relations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, it is often said that foreign policy begins at home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the realities of our external environment and the multiracial character of Singapore, it is a reality that our social compact can be susceptible to fissure and cracks because of geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Beneath the cordial and friendly nature of Singaporeans – the large number of foreigners, our ethnic and racial make-up and the number of new citizens in our economy – can easily be exploited as a fault line.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This may make it more difficult for the population to be psychologically prepared for a far more contentious and unpredictable external environment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have alluded to this prospect at previous Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) agrees that Singaporeans should never allow ourselves to be divided – whether by race, religion, income, social differences or place of birth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality of a far more complex and diverse Singapore than ever before, can make this feel like a tall order.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it would be important to see ourselves as Singaporeans first, ahead of our ethnic differences, even as the latter categories define who we are culturally.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, thank you for the privilege to participate in this COS.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One year ago, Russia launched a full-scale invasion on the small sovereign state of Ukraine.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One year on, the war is still raging.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two years ago, the coup in Myanmar started, and today, the violence is reportedly getting worse.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, geopolitical tensions between the US and China have intensified, and Taiwan, which is the red line for China, is constantly being "put to the test".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, alas, if there were any dreams for peace in the Korean Peninsula post Kim-Trump Summit – those, too, have fast faded into the distance.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have experienced supply chain disruptions since the COVID-19 pandemic and these are further exacerbated by the Russia-Ukraine war, especially for food and energy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Inflation is at a 14-year high, and across the globe, we see increasing protectionism.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, troubling times that we live in.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is a small and young nation in this increasingly divided world where we see sharpened rivalry and deepened mistrust between nations, and even between peoples in the same country.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The "Terror on Capitol Hill" is but a vivid reminder of how mistrust, once sowed, can lead to consequences that one cannot imagine could happen.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans must not think, even for a moment, that these things can never happen to us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, whether it is our National Service or our multicultural, multi-religious heritage or our shared values of building an inclusive and progressive society for all, Singaporeans must always have the courage to speak and act with integrity for our country.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We are a small nation and may, at times, have to walk a tight rope.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is pertinent that Singapore does not falter, but firmly stick to principles and abide by global rules-based multilateral system, whether for international security or for international trade.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore may be small, but as Minister Vivian Balakrishnan often reiterated, and I quote, "We cannot be bought, nor can we be bullied." Our diplomacy approach is simple.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Kudos to our Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) colleagues here and in the overseas Missions for establishing strong diplomatic relationships with many countries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I read with pride The Straits Times article on how our Singapore men from the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) responded to a request by Turkey and took part in the rescue operations in Southern Turkey, which was hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake on 6 February.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is one of the many heartwarming examples of Singapore diplomacy at its best.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Both these superpowers are Singapore's key trading partners with China as Singapore's largest trading partner and the US as Singapore's top foreign investor.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The US is also Singapore's third largest trading partner and Singapore is China's top foreign investor.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In 2022, we are glad to see the high-level engagements that Singapore leaders had with the US and with China.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One, with the US-China geopolitics heating up – to the extent of balloons being shot down, how do we ensure that Singapore, being a little red dot, is not caught in their "bullfight"?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two, in view of recent Presidential-level engagements between them, how hopeful can we be that open communications and dialogue will continue to progress constructively?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Three, how can Singapore build on our strong political and diplomatic engagements with the US and China, as well as with multilateral institutions, to play an effective role as bridge-builder to tackle common challenges, for example, climate change and digital economy?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: How does Singapore's good relations and strong trade with these two superpowers, keep us in the "green lane" with both of them and enable us to not have to take sides?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Both Leaders affirmed the close and multi-faceted relationships between Singapore and China.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The infections have apparently peaked and normalcy has begun to return to major Chinese cities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are reports of foreign businesses gearing up for travel into China as it reopens its door for foreign travellers again.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Can Minister give us an outlook of the Singapore-China relationship in 2023, especially in the post-pandemic era, given the many areas that both countries are keen to work on together?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I note the recent visit to Singapore by the Malaysian Prime Minister, Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There will also be a Leaders' Retreat later this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Singaporean and Malaysian governments often collaborate on external issues of mutual concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We do so in several ways – bilaterally, through ASEAN, or as part of groupings, like the Five Power Defence Arrangements and Strait of Malacca Patrols.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Amid the COVID-19 restrictions, Singaporeans discovered how important Malaysian workers are to our economy, just as Malaysian food products are an integral part of our diet.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Cultural and social currents often flow both ways across our borders as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As neighbours that are geographically right next to each other, there will be differences from time to time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Historically, this included differences over water supply, something that Singapore's diversification of national taps may be helping to alleviate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Then, there are disputes over Pedra Branca, Middle Rocks and South Ledge, which both sides resolved through arbitration at the International Court of Justice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Also appearing as occasional points of disagreement are maritime delimitation, the effects of land reclamation, as well as flight paths for military and civil aircraft.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Generally, both sides seek to address differences professionally and respect the arbitral processes in which they agree to participate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We would, of course, bear in mind the potential for political instability in Malaysia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the areas that he seeks to explore, either bilaterally with the Malaysian government, or even unilaterally, beyond those covered during Datuk Seri Anwar's recent visit?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are there any timelines for these proposals or projects?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the communication channels to prevent the escalation of differences, to ensure calm and professional management and resolution of differences as and when they arise?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This bilateral relationship is one we must manage effectively in an increasingly contested and uncertain world.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I ask the Foreign Minister to lay out the Government's perspective.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, Singapore has excellent ties with Malaysia at the federal level.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Malaysian Prime Minister Dato Seri Anwar Ibrahim recently made an official visit to Singapore in January 2023 where he met both President Halimah and Prime Minister Lee.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, Deputy Prime Minister and Minster for Finance Lawrence Wong's first official visit in his capacity as Deputy Prime Minister was to Malaysia in September 2022.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, Singapore and Brunei have long maintained strong relations and, importantly, support for each other.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the pandemic, Singapore and Brunei had issued a joint Ministerial Statement together with Australia, Canada, Chile, Myanmar and New Zealand affirming commitment to ensuring supply chain connectivity and launched Reciprocal Green Lanes, as well as our first Vaccinated Travel Lanes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As both countries emerged from the pandemic, our high-level and people-to-people exchanges have steadily resumed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, Prime Minister Lee and Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had both visited Brunei, while the Sultan of Brunei and Crown Prince of Brunei have made separate visits to Singapore in August 2022, where they discussed a broad range of areas to further bilateral cooperation in areas, such as in energy and green economy and in youth exchanges.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How have we built on the special Singapore-Brunei bilateral relationship last year, Sultan of Brunei's state visit?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, Indonesia is one of Singapore's closest neighbours.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore and Indonesia are connected through family ties, social and commercial relationships.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As one of our most important bilateral partners, we enjoy a high level of cooperation across a wide range of sectors.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: According to Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI)'s figures released last year, Indonesia is Singapore's sixth largest trading partner.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In June 2022, our Minister for Trade and Industry visited Indonesia to meet with his counterpart among others.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Both sides expressed interest in deepening bilateral cooperation in the areas of energy, infrastructure development and the digital economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister share with the House an update on how Singapore is stepping up cooperation with Indonesia, especially from the economic perspective?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, Singapore and Indonesia have had a long-standing and deep relationship tracing back to the late 1960s, following the end of the Konfrontasi.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Both were founding members of ASEAN and economic ties between both have been deep.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore is the largest foreign investor in Indonesia and both countries are each other's largest source of foreign visitors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The government-to-government and people-to-people ties are strong and close at many levels.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Yet, even between friendly neighbours, there will be differences and matters that need to be resolved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Prime Ministers of both countries meet regularly and try to address these matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We signed the first FIR with Indonesia and the first agreement on military cooperation in 1995.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The military agreement was implemented for a few years and then lapsed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The FIR could not be implemented because of external factors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In 2007, agreements were reached on both defence cooperation and extradition, but these were not ratified by Indonesia at the time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Each of the points that were agreed upon last year give clarity to matters that are important to both countries and were negotiated as part of a framework to create a good balance of benefits for both sides.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: There is an option to renew this delegation beyond 25 years, if both parties wish.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The Defence Cooperation Agreement provided for both governments to ratify and implement the 2007 agreement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This provides for cooperation between the armed forces and also permits the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) to continue training in South China Sea Danger Area, where it had been training since the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This means that the agreements have received the necessary internal support from the Indonesian legislature.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I will be grateful if the Minister can give an update on the status of the implementation of these three agreements and whether anything further needs to be done.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, the situation in Myanmar remains critical and fragile.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The continuing violence in the country remains of deep concern as it also affects neighbouring countries and impacts ASEAN's community-building efforts.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Since the finalisation of ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus in 2021, there has been little progress in its implementation, especially in the area of cessation of violence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This, despite efforts by successive Special Envoys of the ASEAN Chairs, Brunei and Cambodia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As a result, much of the country remains in need of humanitarian assistance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: During the 40th and 41st ASEAN Summits held in November 2022, the leaders called on all parties in Myanmar to facilitate the work of the Secretary-General of ASEAN and ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance in delivering assistance in Myanmar to all in need.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, Sir, ASEAN has come a long way since its establishment in 1967.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: ASEAN has kept the peace among us and gave us collective heft internationally.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To tap on the promise of ASEAN as a dynamic and diverse growth engine, we have developed a comprehensive agenda to expanded collaboration, tackle challenges and seize new opportunity within ourselves and with like-minded external partners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Amidst the geopolitical tensions, ASEAN has stood apart as a region committed to economic freedom, growth and free trade and one that upholds the international rule of law.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yet, ASEAN needs more than inspiring ideals and rousing principles to thrive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must use our collective weight and potential, to encourage key external powers from all over the world to contribute constructively to our growth and stability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In short, ASEAN must be the destination for all and be the backyard of no one.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can our Minister for Foreign Affairs share how Singapore has worked to develop closer integration within ASEAN, and to help ASEAN engage with our external powers?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An effective ASEAN can help countries in the region, including Singapore, to punch above their weight when dealing with major powers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Despite all its benefits, ASEAN's flaws have been laid bare on several occasions, most recently with the crisis in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This requirement can hamper ASEAN's ability to address critical security issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How is Singapore working with ASEAN to overcome situations where consensus is hindered by a minority of member states?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has there ever been any push by Singapore at the ASEAN Summit for a decision to be taken by majority vote on issues, where arriving at a consensus is impossible?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has Singapore asked ASEAN to adopt stronger mechanisms to enforce its own consensus decisions?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does the ASEAN Summit have the authority to decide by a vote to suspend Myanmar from participation in all ASEAN meetings and initiatives?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will send a strong signal to the country's military rulers that their violent actions against their own citizens are not compatible with ASEAN's principles.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last November, the US and ASEAN established a comprehensive strategic partnership at the 10th ASEAN-US Summit in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This new agreement will facilitate closer collaborations in a wide range of areas, including climate change, energy research, transportation and health, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry provide an update on US engagement of ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: ASEAN has been boosting its engagement with more countries over the years, including through the extra-regional platform of ASEAN Plus Three (APT), which comprises 10 ASEAN member states, the People's Republic of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea (ROK).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, APT is the main platform to promote East Asian Cooperation, including political security, trade and investment, finance, energy and many, many more areas.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In view of the rising tensions between the US and China, what are the main challenges facing APT, and how can APT advance to protect and promote the interests of East Asia?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is the APT on track with the implementation of the ASEAN Community Vision 2025?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share recent APT initiatives and their outcomes?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore enjoys good engagement with the Pacific Islands.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have hosted the Pacific Islands FinTech Innovation Challenge in July 2022, which aimed to foster stronger collaboration between ASEAN and the Pacific Islands in digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry share with us which are the areas of cooperation ASEAN and Pacific Islands seek to advance in the near future?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is indicative of a strong partnership between Singapore and India.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, last June, Prime Minister Lee made his first official visit to Africa when he visited Rwanda.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I understand that he had announced a three-year Singapore-Africa Partnership Package.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We have also kept up ties with South Asia.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Several Ministers visited the region last year, including Deputy Prime Minister Wong, who also made an official visit to India in September.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are the plans to step up engagements with emerging markets this year?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, last month, at the 16th Pacific Alliance (PA) Summit in Colombia, Minister for Trade and Industry, Mr Gan Kim Yong, signed the PA-Singapore Free Trade Agreement (PASFTA) and PA-Singapore Joint Declaration with his counterparts from the PA member states – namely, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In July last year, we substantively concluded negotiations with the other Latin America economic bloc, the Southern Common Market (MERCOSUR), which comprises Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry elaborate how these agreements will benefit and help build trade between Singapore and Latin America?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry also share with the House an update on our other initiatives to engage with Latin America?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The MOU aims to jointly promote capacity building in ASEAN and the region.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The European Union (EU) countries like Germany are also keen for more cooperation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: So, what happens there is also important to us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In September 2022, the Minister for Foreign Affairs made an official visit to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia as both countries commemorate the 45th anniversary of diplomatic relations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: During the visit, Minister has also met the Secretary-General of the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf (GCC), His Excellency Dr Nayef Al-Hajraf.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: How is Singapore looking to build on our growing ties with the Gulf countries?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Recently, the Middle East has seen a positive spotlight with Qatar hosting a successful Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) World Cup finals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: There is, thus, opportunity to bring closer people-to-people ties.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, besides such close cooperation with the Gulf countries, what other role can Singapore play in assisting to alleviate the Palestinian-Israeli tensions in the Middle East, whether on our own or together with other Gulf countries?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: More countries are taking steps to shore up their economic security through policies to safeguard strategically important technologies and data.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This development would create more barriers for businesses to internationalise, with a likely negative impact on global economic growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister for his view on how he see globalisation panning out in the years ahead?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We play our part, working with these agencies to deal major crisis and help resolve deep-seated global issues.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister if these multilateral organisations have been able to galvanise actions and make real impact?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Is multilateralism still useful for Singapore when globalisation is under threat and what role should Singapore play?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, Sir, the international situation is in flux.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: One, the war in Ukraine is undermining the international system that kept the peace and defended countries' independence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Two, strained US-China relations have made armed conflict more likely and split up technology, finance and supply chains.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Four, the climate emergency is worsening the differences between countries, leading to greater worldwide inequality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Fortunately, change brings opportunities for those who are bold and fast-moving.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: For example, advancing technology is enabling Singapore to do business with more people further away.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Furthermore, Singapore is at the heart of ASEAN – a large, varied, rapidly growing and youthful region.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Can our Minister for Foreign Affairs explain how we can adjust our foreign policy to ensure that Singapore succeeds in this shifting world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: How can our Foreign Service help us in this?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As Singapore and the rest of the world step down on COVID-19 restrictions, travel is picking up globally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singaporeans have always been well-travelled and "revenge travelling" is expected to fuel even more expected trips for some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is common to hear people saying that they need to make up for lost time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I believe Mr Vikram Nair, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms Janet Ang and the Leader of the Opposition have asked about the impact of the difficult and complicated US-China relationship on our region and on Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This represents, in fact, a fundamental deficit of strategic trust, rooted in incompatible worldviews and aggravated by their respective domestic political pressures.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both sides wish to avoid conflict, but neither side can afford to be seen as weak.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It exacerbated suspicions and tensions amidst strong domestic reactions on both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The incident was a setback to the interactions between the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But I am glad that Secretary of State Antony Blinken and State Councilor Wang Yi did meet in Munich earlier this month.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It shows that both sides recognise the necessity for dialogue and diplomacy, especially at times like these.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Effective communication between the US and China is vital to manage risks in global affairs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both sides need to establish guardrails, as hardened, negative views against the "other side" increasingly become structural features of geopolitical discourse, in both the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For example, there is a growing body of opinion within China that the US is a superpower in terminal decline, which is determined to contain China's rise at all costs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the US, there has also been a deep shift in attitudes towards China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US believes that China "is the only competitor with both the intent to reshape the international order and, increasingly, the economic, diplomatic, military and technological power to advance that objective".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is now a settled bipartisan US view that China's rising power is inimical to American interests and values.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both sides are now locked in an intense and sharpening strategic competition across multiple domains.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US has identified computing-related technologies, biotech and clean tech as force multipliers throughout the technological ecosystem and emphasised leadership in each of these arenas as a national security imperative.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Consequently, the US has decided that it needs to maintain as large a lead as possible over China in these fields.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To this end, the US is implementing systematic measures, including export restrictions on advanced semi-conductor technology.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There are, in fact, ongoing discussions on an outbound investment screening mechanism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On its part, China is determined to achieve greater self-reliance and to prevent itself from being held to ransom.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is progressively onshoring segments of its supply chains in the tech sector.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Collectively, these moves by both sides, increase the danger of a grand bifurcation in technological and economic systems, a deepening of tensions and an elevation of mutual suspicions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These have profound implications for the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is a real risk that the steps taken by the US and China to reduce their mutual interdependence will adversely affect the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our open economy is highly dependent on doing business with the entire world and we have benefited greatly from being a vital node in globalised supply chains.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US is the largest foreign investor in Singapore and our top trading partner for services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we are also one of the largest investors in China, which is our top trading partner in goods.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If the US and China get along, then Singapore will be ideally positioned to prosper.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On the other hand, if things go wrong between them, these strengths can quickly turn into vulnerabilities for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For China, Taiwan is a part of China and Taiwanese independence is an absolute red line.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, to the US and some other western countries, Taiwan is a vibrant democracy that they need to protect, just like Ukraine, which in fact, is different, because Ukraine is an independent country and a member of the UN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Meanwhile in Taiwan, more and more people are identifying themselves as exclusively Taiwanese.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Whilst neither the US nor China seek a military conflict over Taiwan, missteps or mishaps can easily trigger a cycle of "tit-for-tat" actions and reactions that spiral dangerously out of control.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Not only is Taiwan much nearer to us geographically, but our ties with the US, with China and Taiwan are much stronger and deeper, compared to our ties with Russia and Ukraine.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have repeatedly stressed to both the US and China that Singapore and indeed, the countries in our region want to maintain good relations with both countries.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We do not wish to be forced to choose sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We participate in multiple initiatives that have overlapping memberships, but do not always include both parties, for instance, whether you talk about the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework, or the Global Development Initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have always put Singapore's national interest first and we take principled positions impartially, even if it does not always please one or the other superpower.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need the quiet confidence and the national unity to do so consistently, for the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Given the grave implications for the world, we, like most countries, hope that the US and China work out a modus vivendi between themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore has always advocated engaging major players so that they all have a stake in the peace, stability and development of our region, and can create a stable balance of power in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This provides small countries, like Singapore, more room for manoeuvre than if there was only a single power dominating our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Naturally, we do not want the major powers to make Asia their battleground or conduct proxy wars here.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Instead, we want them to be engaged constructively – politically and economically – so as to enhance regional cooperation, development and security.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
